title: COP31: Nepal fails to get Himalayan climate agenda included; major leaders skip Antalya summit - WION
description: COP31: Nepal fails to get Himalayan climate agenda included; major leaders skip Antalya summit  WION

full_article:
A proposal by Nepal, Bhutan and Kyrgyzstan to include mountain climate change as a separate agenda item at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) has failed to secure a place on the formal list of discussions, after it did not receive sufficient backing from developed nations.

The summit began on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, with several world leaders in attendance. However, the absence of prominent figures, including US President Donald Trump and leaders from major European economies, has also drawn attention.

Nepal and Bhutan had jointly submitted a proposal titled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains”, while Kyrgyzstan sought to establish an annual dialogue on mountains and climate change under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Neither proposal was accepted as a separate formal agenda item.

The setback came despite Nepal's efforts to build a broader coalition of mountain countries and bring the growing climate vulnerabilities of the Hindu Kush Himalaya into mainstream international climate negotiations.

According to the Kathmandu Post, the issue has become particularly urgent for Nepal following the August 26 mountain collapse and subsequent floods and landslides in the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system, which caused widespread destruction across several districts.

Addressing the COP31 plenary, Khanal said more than 1,400 people had lost their lives and over 5,000 remained missing. Critical infrastructure was swept away within minutes, while reconstruction costs were estimated at around one-tenth of Nepal's entire economy.

Meanwhile, the absence of several major world leaders has become a talking point at the summit.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are among those attending.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is also expected in Antalya. However, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the summit. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the latest list of attendees.

The United States, under President Trump, has been critical of international climate efforts and has again chosen not to participate. A Nepal resident was arrested with approximately 50 grams of chitta (heroin) near Hatkoti in Shimla district.

The accused has been identified as Sanju Rahi alias Madhav (29), a native of Nepal.

According to the police, a district police team was patrolling near Galu village in Hatkoti when it spotted a suspicious individual. The team stopped him for checking and recovered the contraband from his possession. He was immediately arrested.

Shimla SSP Gaurav Singh, confirmed the arrest and said that a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 has been registered against the accused. Further investigation is under way.

title: Hong Kong and Nepal ties historically rooted - Nepali Times
description: Hong Kong and Nepal ties historically rooted  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The first trip one of us undertook to Kathmandu was two months ago, for the Nepal Economic Forum.

The forum showed the diversity of thought, richness of culture, and resilience of national character that defined the Nepali people. Some of the interlocutors that this country of 30 million cannot be reduced to its capital region.

A 30,000 strong Nepali diaspora resides and works in Hong Kong, many in the hospitality and service sectors. Their professionalism, congeniality, and linguistic dexterity render them a much-needed component of the city’s workforce.

Such a relationship between our two economies is by not incidental: it is historically rooted in the legacy of the British rule in Hong Kong and the presence of Gurkha soldiers, who served in the territory for five decades, between 1948-1997.

As Nepal looks to engage the world on renewed terms of “developmental autonomy”, in the words of its Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal. Hong Kong is uniquely positioned to serve as a constructive interlocutor and partner for the country.

As an open and advanced economy, Hong Kong has established and adapted to historical trade winds. As Nepal seeks to formalise and harness the full dividends from its cross-border trade with India and China, challenges such as transaction hurdles and under-utilisation of zero-tariff quotas demand more attention to system designs underpinning the flow of goods.

Hong Kong-based lawyers and supply chain experts can provide grounded advice on how Nepali merchants can make use of the Chinese market, especially on specialty goods such as coffee and high-value raw and plant-based medical materials, which serve as core ingredients of traditional Chinese medicines.

The Special Administrative Region is well-suited to provide legal and regulatory counsel to Nepali trading companies looking to grasp and engage China better. It should also facilitate closer communication and liaison between private Chinese capital seeking to invest in overseas destinations especially in the healthcare, recreation, and tourism industries, and projects in Nepal, whilst upholding the crucial quality and standards that ensure genuine buy-in from the local community.

title: Nepal Expands Open-Source Electronic Medical Records Across Nineteen Public Hospitals - Bioengineer.org
description: Nepal Expands Open-Source Electronic Medical Records Across Nineteen Public Hospitals  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Nineteen government hospitals across six of Nepal’s seven provinces have transitioned to functional open-source electronic medical records, establishing integrated digital systems across multiple clinical departments. According to a community case study published in Frontiers in Digital Health, the phased deployments replaced paper records with longitudinal patient files accessible across departments, integrated laboratory and radiology results, established standardized electronic reporting, and expanded routine data available for oversight.

The health systems implementation was documented by Dipendra Gautam and colleagues from the World Health Organization country office in Nepal and the Ministry of Social Development and Health of Gandaki Province. In their assessment, the authors noted that many public hospitals in low- and middle-income countries still depend on paper documentation, which fragments patient histories, duplicates diagnostic procedures, and limits routine data essential for health management and policy planning.

Nepal’s transition toward open-source digital health platforms began in the early 2010s, utilizing Bahmni, an electronic medical record platform built on OpenMRS, as a license-free and locally adaptable alternative to proprietary software. Adoption accelerated following the COVID-19 pandemic and was reinforced by Nepal’s 2022 Joint External Evaluation and COVID-19 Intra-Action Review, both of which called for transitioning away from fragmented paper-based reporting toward integrated digital architectures.

From 2024, legacy installations were upgraded to the FHIR-aligned OpenMRS 3 interface.

Across the participating hospitals, health workers reported improvements in clinical continuity and efficiency, though the study authors noted these gains were reported by users rather than formally measured through quantitative clinical evaluations.

Reflecting on transferable lessons for comparable low- and middle-income settings, the authors concluded that public hospital transitions to electronic medical records represent organizational transformations requiring human and institutional change, rather than purely technological upgrades.

The broader case study contextualizes Nepal’s national implementation within global targets for universal health coverage and health-system resilience.

title: The Evolution of Nepali Banking: A Journey Through Seven Milestones - Ratopati
description: The Evolution of Nepali Banking: A Journey Through Seven Milestones  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Today, any Nepali citizen can transfer lakhs of rupees in seconds by simply swiping their finger on a smartphone. Paying at a store by scanning a QR code or withdrawing and depositing money from a bank account at any time is no longer a novelty.

It is now possible to deposit money using machines, not just withdraw it. The arrival of banking services to this stage has involved Nepali banking navigating through significant ups and downs. In the recent past, banking in Nepal was quite difficult. From having to wait for 3 to 4 hours after taking a token at the bank to exchange a simple check, and then spending time wandering on the streets, Nepali banking has come a long way.

Looking at the 87-year journey since the establishment of Nepal Bank in 1997 BS, the Nepali economy and financial system have progressed through numerous fluctuations, policy experiments, and structural changes, says banking expert and former president of the Nepal Bankers Association, Bhuwan Dahal.

Nepal's banking history is not limited to traditional banking; it has served as the backbone of the economy, from monetizing to preserve the country's sovereignty to today's digitalization.

Here are the details of the main '7 turns' that have transformed Nepali banking history, from the establishment of Nepal Bank to the current paradoxical situation of excess liquidity.

Turn 1: Foundation of Formal Banking and the Battle for Monetization (1997-2013 BS)

Nepal Bank Limited was established in the era of then Rana Prime Minister Juddha Shamsher, inaugurated by King Tribhuvan on Kartik 30, 1997 BS. This was the starting point of Nepal's formal banking history. At that time, due to a lack of technical knowledge for opening a bank, a technical cooperation agreement was made with Imperial Bank of India (now State Bank of India).

Before that, around 1989 BS, the Tejarath Adda provided loans to government employees, but there was no modern institution for the general public to deposit and borrow money. In 2002 BS, the first paper notes were issued from the Sadar Muluki Khana, which were called 'Kagaji Mohar'.

However, the foundation of true financial independence was laid only after the establishment of Nepal Rastra Bank on Baisakh 14, 2013 BS. According to banking expert Bhuwan Dahal, the initial main responsibility of the Rastra Bank was to monetize the country.

He said, 'Before the establishment of the Rastra Bank, the Nepali rupee was not accepted at all in the Terai-Madhesh region of Nepal. The Indian Rupee was like an undeclared legal tender there.'

On one hand, the Rastra Bank established the Nepali rupee as the sole legal currency throughout the country, and on the other hand, it protected financial sovereignty by setting a stable exchange rate between the Nepali currency and the Indian Rupee.



Turn 2: Government Monopoly and Institutional Credit Reaching Villages (2013-2040 BS)

After the establishment of the central bank, the government created other institutions for the development and commercial sectors. In 2016 BS, Nepal Industrial Development Corporation (NIDC) was established, followed by the fully government-owned Rastriya Banijya Bank in 2022 BS, and Krishi Bikas Bank in 2024 BS.

This period was entirely an era of government monopoly and a controlled economy. Banks were more like instruments for implementing the government's socio-economic plans rather than profit-oriented entities. However, during this period, the banking sector brought about a major revolution that touched the lives of Nepalis—the expansion of agricultural credit.

According to Dahal, around 2037/38 BS, Krishi Bikas Bank initiated intensive agricultural banking and the Small Farmers Development Project.

Dahal said, branches of Nepal Bank and Banijya Bank were limited to district headquarters. Poor farmers in the villages had no awareness that they could get loans from banks. It was only after Krishi Bikas Bank started going to the villages and providing small loans for raising buffaloes and buying seeds that the general public began to connect with the banking system.

This program was the first successful attempt to steer farmers away from the exploitative interest rates of informal moneylenders towards institutional credit.



Turn 3: Era of Liberalization, Foreign Joint Ventures, and Customer Service (2041-2050 BS)

In the mid-1940s BS, Nepal adopted policies of open market economy and financial liberalization. As a result, in 2041 BS (1984 AD), Nabil Bank (formerly Nepal Arab Bank) was established as Nepal's first joint venture private bank. Subsequently, Nepal Indo-Suez Bank (now Nepal Investment Mega Bank) was established in 2043 BS, and Nepal Grindlays Bank (now Standard Chartered Bank) in 2044 BS.

This was the biggest paradigm shift in Nepali banking. The entry of foreign banks brought managerial efficiency and modern work practices.

Recalling his early experiences, Dahal says, 'To get a loan in a government bank, you had to please the manager, and you had to wait in line for hours to get service. But after the private joint venture banks arrived, the marketing concept that the customer is god for the bank finally emerged. Banks even started the practice of inviting customers for tea-coffee and dinner parties.'

During this period, concepts like the single teller system where checks could be cashed at a single counter, rapid fund transfers through fax and telegraphic transfers, modern letters of credit (LC) for international trade, bank guarantees, and consortium loans for large infrastructure projects were institutionalized. This directly connected Nepali banking with the international financial market.

Turn 4: Whirlwind of Crisis and the 'Financial Sector Reform Program' (Late 2050s BS - 2065 BS)

In stark contrast to the rapid progress of private banks, government banks deteriorated due to political interference and weak governance.

By the end of the 2050s BS, the non-performing loans of Nepal Bank Limited and Rastriya Banijya Bank had reached a staggering 50 to 60 percent. As these two large banks were technically on the verge of bankruptcy, the entire financial system faced the threat of collapse.

To overcome that crisis, the government and Nepal Rastra Bank, with the support of the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, launched the much-discussed Financial Sector Reform Program starting in 2058 BS. This was the fourth decisive turn in Nepali banking history.

This program primarily focused on four areas.

1. Autonomous Act – The central bank was made autonomous and powerful by issuing the Nepal Rastra Bank Act, 2058 BS.

2. Foreign Management – The management of Nepal Bank was handed over to foreign consultants, and the management of Rastriya Banijya Bank was entrusted to American consultants.

3. Write-off and Revival – The recovery of billions of rupees in bad loans given under political pressure was aggressively pursued, staff were reduced, and both banks were revived. NIDC was later merged into Rastriya Banijya Bank.

According to expert Dahal, this reform program not only saved Nepal's financial system from disaster but also established modern risk management and strict regulatory standards permanently.



Turn 5: Flood of Numbers, Shock of Capital Increase, and Big Mergers (2065-2079 BS)

As the liberalization policy loosened, the Rastra Bank liberally distributed licenses for banks and financial institutions in the 2060s BS. As a result, in a small economy with a population of 25 million, the number of financial institutions, including classes 'A', 'B', 'C', and 'D', exceeded 250.

Due to excessive unhealthy competition, reckless lending in real estate, and weak institutional governance, many finance companies and development banks fell into crisis. To curb this anomaly, Nepal Rastra Bank took two strategic steps.

First, in 2068 BS, the Merger Bylaws were introduced to encourage institutions to merge. The second and most powerful shock was delivered by then Governor Dr. Chiranjibi Nepal through the monetary policy in 2072 BS. He introduced a mandatory policy to quadruple the paid-up capital of 'A' class commercial banks from 2 billion to 8 billion rupees at once.

This policy caused an earthquake in the banking sector. To meet the capital requirements, banks were forced to issue rights shares, bonus shares, and especially to merge with each other. In the following years, by the tenure of Governor Maha Prasad Adhikari, the 'big merger' of commercial banks merging with each other intensified.

At one time, the number of commercial banks reached 32, but today it has reduced to 20. This has reduced the number of financial institutions, strengthening the capital base, enabling investment in large projects, and increasing risk-bearing capacity.



Turn 6: Leap in Technology – From Ledger, Token, and SWIFT to Digital Ecosystem (from the 2040s BS to the present)

Although the development of technology in Nepali banking has been a long evolutionary process, the impact it has created is no less than a revolution.



Delving into its journey...





From Ledgers to Standalone Computers – Until the 2040s BS, the ledger system was in use. Although Nabil Bank introduced computers, initially each branch had its own standalone computer, and the branches were not interconnected.

ATMs and Branch Networks – Dahal recalls that Himalayan Bank and Nabil Bank introduced ATMs in the mid-1990s. Initially, when Nabil Bank installed an ATM at its Kantipath branch, only customers of the Kantipath branch could use that ATM card. Customers of other branches could not, as the branches were not yet connected online.

Arrival of ABBS and SWIFT – When the Any Branch Banking System (ABBS) and centralized Core Banking Software (CBS) arrived via telephone lines and optical fiber, customers could withdraw money from any branch. The secure SWIFT system was implemented, replacing telegraphic transfers (which carried a high risk of messages getting garbled or lost) in international transactions.

Smartphone and QR Revolution – The decade after 2072 BS became a decade of explosive digital banking. Nepal Clearing House's ConnectIPS, mobile banking, wallets (eSewa, Khalti, etc.), and QR codes have significantly reduced the use of paper notes in retail payments. Today, cashless transactions, from vegetable shops to large shopping malls, have become an integral part of daily life.

Turn 7: Federal Financial Access and the Current Paradox – The Crisis of Excess Liquidity (2074 BS to present)

With the promulgation of Nepal's constitution in 2072 BS and the country's transition to federalism, the seventh turn in the banking sector began. The government and the Rastra Bank adopted a mandatory policy to establish at least one commercial bank branch in all 753 local levels of the country.

Before 2074 BS, banks were present in only 20-25 percent of local levels. Citizens in remote villages had to walk all day to the district headquarters to receive social security allowances or conduct simple government transactions. Today, commercial bank branches have reached almost all local levels. This has expanded financial inclusion and the formal economy to the villages.

However, at this seventh turn, a strange paradoxical crisis, never before seen in Nepali banking history, has emerged—an abundance of investable funds but a drought in loan demand.

Currently, there is more than 65 trillion rupees in deposits in banks. Trillions of rupees are piled up in the banking system. The Rastra Bank has foreign exchange reserves of over 26 billion US dollars, which can cover about a year and a half of imports. Deposit interest rates have fallen below the inflation rate.

'In a poor country like ours with a per capita income of $1400-1500, it is a management failure and policy inertia that trillions of rupees are lying idle instead of being invested,' said Dahal, who is also a member of the High-Level Financial Sector Reform Suggestion Committee formed by the Ministry of Finance. 'We have not been able to utilize the remaining 16 billion dollars when 10 billion dollars of foreign exchange reserves would suffice. We have cement, iron, and manpower within the country, but infrastructure projects are stalled.'

Today, banks have ample capital to lend, but due to a lack of confidence in the private sector, there is no demand for loans. The challenge of how to mobilize this idle capital into infrastructure, energy, tourism, and productive sectors has become the seventh and most complex turn in today's banking landscape.

Nepal Celebrates Bhai Tika

Author: Arvind Jain

People Celebrate Bhai Tika Festival In Kathmandu, Nepal People without brothers or sisters receive tika from women during the Bhai Tika festival at Rani Pokhari in Kathmandu, Nepal, on November 11, 2026. The tradition allows those without siblings to receive tika and blessings during Tihar. (Photo by Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Nepal is celebrating Bhai Tika today, marking the concluding day of its five-day festival of Tihar. The occasion celebrates the special bond between brothers and sisters and is observed with traditional rituals and prayers. On this occasion, sisters apply colourful five or seven-coloured tika on their brothers’ foreheads and pray for their long life, good health and prosperity. In Kathmandu, the historic Balgopaleshwor Temple at Rani Pokhari opened its doors to devotees on the occasion. Despite rainfall, devotees visited the temple to offer prayers and receive tika and blessings. The temple opens to the public only once a year, on Bhai Tika. People who do not have brothers or sisters come here to observe the festival and receive tika from the priests. The five or seven colours of the tika symbolise good fortune, happiness and prosperity. With Bhai Tika, the five-day festival of Tihar comes to an end across Nepal. Arvind Jain, IIS (PBSC, All India Radio & Doordarshan, Kathmandu)
